title: Future forms
tagline: Six ways to talk about what comes next, from a plan already fixed to a prediction based on evidence.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations
Listening Part 4 — multiple choice (plans, predictions, intentions)
Writing Part 1 — essay: consequences and the future of an issue
why: English doesn't have one future tense — it has several, and the choice signals how certain or how fixed the plan is. B2 First tests whether you can tell a spontaneous decision (will) from a firm intention (going to) from a diary arrangement (present continuous), plus the special time-clause rule that bans will after when and as soon as.

rows.label: Typical use
cells: offers, promises, predictions with no evidence

diagrams.title: No will after time words

parts.chip: when / as soon as / before / until

diagrams.caption: The future time clause takes the present simple, even though the whole sentence is about the future.

head: Form
Use
Example
rows: will + infinitive
a decision made now, an offer, a promise, a prediction with no evidence
I think it'll be a close match.
going to + infinitive
an intention decided earlier, a prediction with evidence now
Look at those clouds — it's going to pour.
present continuous
a fixed arrangement, with a time and often another person
We're seeing the dentist on Thursday.
present simple
a timetable, a programme, an official schedule
The train departs at 9.15.
future continuous
an action in progress at a stated time in the future
This time next week, we'll be sitting the exam.
future perfect
an action finished before a stated point in the future
By July, she'll have finished her portfolio.
be about to / be likely to
very soon / probability
We're about to start. / Prices are likely to rise.
Time clauses (when, as soon as, until, before)
present simple, never will, even though the meaning is future
As soon as I hear the results, I'll text you.

use.point: Plans, intentions and predictions with evidence

examples.text: Mateo is going to apply for the exchange programme next year.

use.point: A point in the future: continuous, perfect and time clauses

watch_out.wrong: When I will arrive, I will call you.
watch_out.right: When I arrive, I will call you.
watch_out.why: Time clauses with when, as soon as, before, until take the present simple, never will.

watch_out.wrong: I'm going to the cinema this weekend — I decided this right now.
watch_out.right: I'll go to the cinema this weekend.
watch_out.why: A decision made at the moment of speaking needs will, not going to, which suggests an earlier plan.

watch_out.wrong: Look at those dark clouds — it will rain.
watch_out.right: Look at those dark clouds — it's going to rain.
watch_out.why: A prediction based on evidence you can see now uses going to, not will.

watch_out.wrong: By next year I will finish the course.
watch_out.right: By next year I will have finished the course.
watch_out.why: An action completed before a future point needs the future perfect, not will + infinitive.

watch_out.wrong: This time next week we will go skiing.
watch_out.right: This time next week we 'll be going skiing.
watch_out.why: An action in progress at a stated future moment needs the future continuous.

watch_out.wrong: We meeting Miss Vega at four tomorrow.
watch_out.right: We're meeting Miss Vega at four tomorrow.
watch_out.why: A fixed personal arrangement needs the auxiliary be before the present continuous.

dialogue.title: Planning the trip to the coast
dialogue.context: Sofia, Mateo and Liam are working out the last details for a weekend trip while Miss Vega checks the schedule.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Right, so what time does the bus leave on Saturday?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: It leaves at seven sharp, according to the official timetable.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Perfect. I 'm going to pack everything tonight so I'm not rushing in the morning.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Good idea. I'll probably forget something anyway, knowing me.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: As soon as we arrive, we'll drop our bags and head straight for the beach.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: By the time you get there, the tide will have gone out, so watch your step on the rocks.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Noted. Oh — look at those clouds. It's going to rain before we even leave.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Don't worry, I'll bring an umbrella just in case.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: This time tomorrow, we'll be lying on the sand instead of sitting in class.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Can't wait. I promise I won't complain once, not even about the early start.

summary: Will: a decision made now, an offer, a promise, or a prediction with no evidence.
Going to: an intention decided earlier, or a prediction based on evidence you can see.
Present continuous: a fixed personal arrangement; present simple: an official timetable.
Future continuous: in progress at a future moment; future perfect: finished before a future point.
After when, as soon as, before, until, the verb stays in the present simple — never will.
